claims.text: Thermal aging causes microstructural evolution in non-equilibrium high-entropy alloys.
During aging, Mg diffuses out of the homogeneous solid solution and segregates.
Mg segregation produces fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, especially at grain boundaries.
Precipitates can alter properties of high-entropy alloys.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates act as preferential nucleation sites for protective oxides such as Mg-Al spinels.
Precipitate-assisted formation of a more protective oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aging-induced local compositional gradients generate galvanic effects.
The resulting galvanic effects alter aqueous corrosion currents and potentials relative to the as-quenched state.
The initial as-quenched alloy is metastable and has a homogeneous solid solution with uniformly distributed Mg.
Minor undifferentiated intermetallic phases may already be present in the initial state.
Aging at intermediate to high temperatures, exemplified by 700-900 °C, is sufficient to activate the proposed Mg diffusion and phase evolution.
Compared with the as-quenched control, an aged sample will contain a detectably greater population of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Compared with the as-quenched control, an aged sample will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain or a thinner, more protective oxide scale.
The as-quenched baseline forms a less effective protective oxide scale than the aged state.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with density below 6 g/cm3.
The mechanism requires enough thermal activation for Mg diffusion while remaining below conditions that cause complete equilibration or excessive grain coarsening.
The mechanism may cease to apply when Mg-alloy chemistry differs substantially or when aging temperature is too low or too high.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as a homogeneous solid solution while also allowing pre-existing intermetallics; the baseline more categorically describes retention of a homogeneous solid solution without significant precipitate formation. This leaves the starting phase constitution ambiguous.
